title: Chatflow pipeline timings and dollar roughs — pipeline-level benchmark sketch
content:
Purpose and quick context:
This is a lightweight working sketch to capture pipeline-level latency and $/token roughs for the 'chatflow' path (client -> front proxy -> router -> model shard / variant -> postprocess). Not a polished report — notes, quick ASCII charts, and open questions. Intended for Console + Tooling folks to decide whether to recommend streaming-by-chunk vs full-response generation for interactive chat apps.

Test matrix (short):
- Models: open-psi-13b (fp16), gptx-14b-quant (8-bit), redwood-mini-7b (fp16)
- Hardware: H100 (dense), A100-80GB (dense), V100-equivalent (old) for baseline
- Modes: streaming-by-chunk (stream increments back to client), fullframe (generate then return), multiplexed-schedule (slotized small tasks on shared workers)
- Request shape: 1 prompt, mean output length 80 tokens (q95 420), prefix cached 40 tokens on repeated sessions
- Batch window: 0 ms (on-demand) vs 8 ms vs 24 ms

Measurement note: wall-clock p50/p90/p99 measured at proxy-level (client RTT excluded). Cost normalized to $ per 1M generated tokens (excluding client tokens) given internal spot GPU hourly price assumptions (H100 effective $3.2/hr after amortization, A100 $2.4/hr). These are internal roughs for directional comparison only.

ASCII summary table (directional):
Mode                 | model         | hw    | p50 ms | p90 ms | p99 ms | tok/s | $/1M gen toks
---------------------+---------------+-------+--------+--------+--------+-------+--------------
streaming-by-chunk   | open-psi-13b  | H100  | 120    | 350    | 930    | 1,100 | 46
fullframe            | open-psi-13b  | H100  | 90     | 260    | 780    | 1,350 | 42
multiplexed-schedule | open-psi-13b  | H100  | 160    | 420    | 1,200  | 950   | 36
streaming-by-chunk   | gptx-14b-q8   | A100  | 140    | 380    | 1,050  | 1,000 | 34
fullframe            | gptx-14b-q8   | A100  | 100    | 300    | 800    | 1,250 | 31
fullframe            | redwood-mini7b| V100  | 70     | 210    | 620    | 1,600 | 55

Interpretation notes:
- Fullframe tends to win median latency by eliminating the per-chunk commit/wakeup overhead, but p99s are still high if long outputs or cold KV cache misses occur.
- Streaming introduces small per-chunk latencies (serialize+send) that compound; for short responses (<50 tokens) streaming can add 30–60ms extra overhead. For longer responses streaming hides perceived latency to user since first token appears earlier.
- Multiplexed scheduling reduced nominal $/1M tokens in these runs because we accepted slightly higher median latency in exchange for higher slot packing (more concurrency), but p99 degradation is material for SLO-sensitive tiers.
- Quantized model on A100 shows good $/token improvement vs fp16 on H100, but tail latency still worse than A100 fullframe fp16 on H100 in some shapes (likely due to kernel fragmentation and memory-copy overhead).

Rough cost assumptions (for these calculations):
- H100 effective cost: $3.2/hr (amortized reserved pricing internal)
- A100 effective cost: $2.4/hr
- Effective tokens generated per GPU-second estimated from observed tok/s and average GPU utilization during the run (accounted for overheads): e.g., open-psi-13b on H100 fullframe ~1,350 tok/s -> ~4.86M tokens/hr per GPU -> $3.2 / 4.86M toks = $0.66 per 1M gen toks (but we add 60% platform overhead -> $1.05). The table above shows consolidated numbers including infra overhead, routing, and infer-queue inefficiencies.

Mini ASCII latency distribution sketch (p0..p100 buckets approximate, streaming-by-chunk open-psi-13b H100):
[median]..........|######...................... (120ms)
[p90]......................|###########......... (350ms)
[p99]................................|#### (930ms)

Key behavior traces observed (anecdotal):
- Many p99 spikes correlate with KV cache misses for long-context sessions; when prefix hit rate drops below ~60% the mean token throughput for that GPU drops 18–30%.
- Serialization pause: the grpc->http translation layer adds 6–14ms per chunk in streaming mode; with 4 chunks average that is ~20–40ms additional to tail.
- Batch windowing at 8ms often improved throughput by ~8–12% while only adding median 6–8ms; good sweet spot for interactive workloads.

Open questions / next steps (practical):
- Re-run with realistic client-side backpressure pattern (clients that pause and resume) — streaming advantages may be amplified or erased depending on chunk cadence.
- Capture GPU-side kernel launch overhead traces (nvtx/instrumentation) for quantized model; suspect extra memcpy between host device for some kernels.
- Repeat multiplexed-schedule runs with stricter p99 SLO on job admission to see if Dollars/1M changes significantly when we enforce tail constraints.
- Add a small experiment: prefix-cache priming (force-hot) vs lazy cache to quantify cold-priming cost per-session.

Suggested messaging (internal one-liner to product marketing):
"For typical short-to-mid chat responses (<150 tokens), fullframe on reserve H100s gives slightly better median latency and simpler SLOs; streaming shines for perceived latency on long responses but needs careful chunk sizing and cache priming to avoid tail surprises. Our tooling should recommend 8ms batch windows and reveal per-route p99 exposure when streaming is enabled."

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Attach raw trace files: TOOL-887/traces/2028-03-12/*. Need to upload to confluence.
- Make a follow-up run focusing on 80/20 session mix — 80% short (<50 tokens), 20% long (>300 tokens) and collect user perceived-first-byte latencies.
- Clean up cost model (this doc uses internal fudge factors). Formalize in product/optimize cost model if directionally consistent.

End of sketch.

-- Maya
